en: Theragāthā 10.3 Dasakanipāta,
Paṭhamavagga (First Chapter)
The Stanzas of the Elder Mahākappina:
“He who, acting with foresight, perceives both the future—
both that which is beneficial and that which is harmful;”
Even outsiders who seek his welfare do not see any flaw in him when they examine him closely—
this is the case for one whose mindfulness is fixed on breathing.
Fully perfected and well-developed,
gradually accumulated just as taught by the Buddha.
He illuminates the world like the moon freed from clouds:
"Truly, my mind is pure."
Immeasurable and well-developed,
having broken through and been uplifted,
it illuminates all directions.
Even if one's wealth is exhausted,
the wise person still lives; yet through the lack of wisdom, [one does not].
Even one who possesses wealth does not truly live.
Wisdom discerns what has been heard;
wisdom increases fame and renown.
A person endowed with wisdom in this world finds happiness even amidst sufferings.
This is not a doctrine of today alone.
It is neither wonderful nor marvelous;
for where one is born and dies,
what indeed could be marvelous there?
For immediately after being born,
death from life is certain;
those who are born here, being born again and again, must die.
For living beings are of such a nature.
This is not for the sake of one who has died,
nor is it for the sake of others' lives, that [one's own life] exists.
Weeping for the dead brings neither fame nor worldly merit;
it is not praised by recluses and brahmins.
For it harms the eye and the body.
One's beauty, strength, and wisdom decline; though they may be joyful toward him,
those who seek his welfare do not find happiness.
Therefore, one should indeed desire to dwell in a family that has both wise and learned members,
for it is by means of their excellence of wisdom that one's purpose is accomplished.
“They cross over as if by boat across a full river,” said the Elder Mahākappina.
